item.title: Green card, no vote: Two Indians face US election fraud charges
item.description: Kaur, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and cast a ballot in the November 2024 election. The department has said that the ...
item.dc:creator: Sunainaa Chadha
item.content:encoded: Two Indian nationals, Amandeep Kaur, 30, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, are among 28 lawful permanent residents charged with alleged election-related offences in California, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ). The charges relate to allegedly registering to vote or casting ballots in US elections despite not being US citizens.  The charges were announced on October 19 as part of “Operation Protect the Vote”, a coordinated enforcement initiative involving all four US attorney’s offices in California. Federal authorities said 11 of the 28 accused were arrested in early-morning operations across the state. The DOJ's announcement did not establish whether Kaur and Shah were among those arrested.  The allegations are criminal charges, not findings of guilt. The case also comes amid a wider dispute between the Trump administration and California officials over the federal government's claims that thousands of potentially ineligible people appear on the state's voter rolls. What are the allegations against the two Indian nationals?According to the DOJ, Shah, a resident of Sacramento, allegedly registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 US general election and cast a ballot that day. Kaur, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and cast a ballot in the November 2024 election. The department has said that the two are among the 28 green card holders charged in the case.  The charges include allegations involving false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration. The DOJ said the defendants appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people it had identified as likely non-citizen registrants and shared with California election officials. That list is part of a separate, broader dispute over voter eligibility and should not be interpreted as proof that every person identified committed an offence.  Can green card holders vote in US elections?No. A green card allows a foreign national to live and work permanently in the United States, but it does not confer US citizenship or the right to vote in federal elections. California's Secretary of State lists US citizenship as a basic requirement for voter registration. Applicants must also be California residents and meet the applicable age and other eligibility requirements. The state's registration process requires applicants to affirm their US citizenship.  Federal law also prohibits non-citizens from voting in elections held to choose the US president, vice-president and members of Congress. Under Section 611 of Title 18 of the US Code, unlawful voting by a non-citizen can carry a fine, imprisonment of up to one year, or both. Certain other election contests may be governed by separate state or local rules, but that does not permit non-citizens to vote for federal offices.  What penalties could the accused face?The DOJ said the charges in the California cases include making false statements in naturalisation applications and, in some cases, fraudulent voter registration. The department said the felony charges carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison. The precise charges and potential penalties depend on the allegations against each defendant.  The distinction between the charges matters. Allegedly voting unlawfully, registering fraudulently and making false statements in an application for citizenship are separate forms of conduct and may attract different penalties under different statutes. For people applying for naturalisation, an allegation involving a false statement can also raise questions about their eligibility for citizenship. However, the consequences for any individual will depend on the evidence, the charges ultimately pursued and the outcome of the legal proceedings. Why has California become the focus of the investigation?The arrests come just weeks before the November 3, 2026, US midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and decide a range of state and local contests. On October 15, the DOJ sued California, asking a federal court to prevent the state from counting mail-in ballots associated with more than 20,000 people whom federal authorities believe may be non-citizens, until their immigration status can be verified. The department said it identified the individuals by comparing publicly available voter-registration information with federal government databases. The dispute escalated after federal officials said California had not agreed to set aside the ballots while the eligibility of the individuals was checked. California conducts elections by mail and sends ballots to registered voters. The federal government is seeking court intervention to ensure that ballots it considers potentially ineligible are not counted.  The list of more than 20,000 people is, however, a list of individuals the federal government considers likely non-citizens. It is not a judicial finding that every person on the list registered unlawfully or voted illegally. What does California say?California officials have disputed the federal government's broader claims and defended the state's election safeguards. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said there was no widespread voter fraud in the state, while acknowledging that individual cases could occur. Secretary of State Shirley Weber has also criticised the federal government's attempts to obtain voter data and said the state's safeguards against non-citizen voting were robust.  There is also a concern about the accuracy of citizenship checks. Reuters reported that voting-rights advocates have warned that outdated federal immigration records could wrongly flag some naturalised US citizens as non-citizens. A person who has become a US citizen through naturalisation is eligible to register to vote if they meet the other requirements; an immigration database that has not been updated may not accurately reflect that person's current status.  An Associated Press report on the California arrests noted that non-citizen voting is considered rare and has not been shown to change election outcomes. Reuters reported on October 15 that its review of prosecutions under the federal law criminalising non-citizen voting had found 129 people prosecuted since the statute was enacted in 1996. Reuters also cited research indicating that instances of non-citizen voting are rare relative to the country's overall electorate.  The DOJ, meanwhile, has stepped up investigations and prosecutions. It said on October 19 that it had charged 28 people in California in the latest operation. AP reported that the department had charged 113 people across 20 states with illegal voting or registration offences over the preceding seven weeks. These figures describe enforcement activity, not the total number of people proven to have voted unlawfully.  What happens next?The 28 defendants will face criminal proceedings, where prosecutors will have to establish the allegations against each person. The DOJ's announcement said the 11 people arrested were expected to make initial appearances in federal courts on October 19, with no pleas to be taken at those appearances.  Separately, the federal lawsuit against California will determine whether the state can be compelled to set aside or verify ballots linked to the people identified by federal authorities. The outcome could affect the balance between federal election-enforcement efforts and states' responsibility for administering elections. For the two Indian nationals, the central issue is whether prosecutors can prove the specific allegations against them. Their status as green card holders does not itself constitute an offence; the allegations concern their reported registration and voting activity.

item.title: Australian govt to sue Facebook, TikTok for alleged breaches of ban
item.description: The country's online safety regulator, eSafety Commissioner, said in March it was investigating Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube for potentially failing to adhere to the law ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Angus Whitley Australia’s government is set to sue Facebook, TikTok and other major digital platforms for alleged non-compliance with a nationwide social media ban for under-16s, Communications Minister Anika Wells said in an interview. The country’s online safety regulator, eSafety Commissioner, said in March it was investigating Facebook and Instagram — both owned by Meta Platforms Inc. — TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube for potentially failing to adhere to the law. The legislation requires the companies to take reasonable steps to stop underage users from holding social media accounts, part of a bid to protect them from harmful online content. In an interview in Sydney on Monday, Wells said she expected legal action to proceed against the five platforms. An eSafety report in July found most underage social media users were able to keep their accounts or create new ones, largely due to a lack of effective age checks on the platforms. Since Australia’s world-first ban came into force almost a year ago, the government has doubled the maximum penalty for breaches to A$109.2 million ($76 million). The government also granted eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant greater investigative powers, including the ability to demand documents from social media platforms and summon current or ex-employees to answer questions. “Now she has more powers to be able to gather the evidence that she needs to take those five companies to the Federal Court,” Wells said. “She’s now using those powers to prepare her case.” Spokespersons for Meta and eSafety had no immediate comments. Representatives for Snapchat owner Snap Inc., TikTok and its owner ByteDance Ltd., and YouTube parent Google didn’t immediately reply to emails seeking responses to the minister’s comments. The eSafety Commissioner is an independent regulator, though part of the government and accountable to Australia’s parliament through the communications minister, a position currently held by Wells. Last week Wells said companies aren’t doing enough to adhere to social media age restrictions. “The law is not failing — platforms are failing to comply with the law,” Wells said in an Oct. 15 speech to the National Press Club. “We won’t flinch at holding tech companies to account.”

item.description: SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about $30 billion ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO

OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about $30 billion

OpenAI's funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters NEW YORK 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 11:05 AM IST

Listen to This Article

OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic's expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over $1.4 trillion, according to two people familiar with the matter.   The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping in to a similar investor base, the people said, adding that OpenAI wants to capitalize on its recent revenue growth after launching new models.    SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about $30 billion, one of the people said.

The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of AI valuations.   OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI's funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said. Also Read

OpenAI staffer accused of planting recording device in office denied bail

Jio IPO anchor book sees over 30x demand, draws record bids worth ₹2.5 trn

IPO offer document: What to read, what to skip when assessing fundamentals

OpenAI poaches another SpaceX sales lead for cybersecurity business

India is shaping how OpenAI builds products, says CTO Vijaye Raji premium

Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the IPO markets further delays its planned 2027 listing.

Though there is high demand for the shares of both companies, investors face the challenge of evaluating and allocating capital to two complex, competing offerings within days or weeks of each other. Some investors view OpenAI's financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic's IPO, the people said.   OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment.  TRYING TO HEAD OFF COMPARISONS   OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached $50 billion in annualized revenue and expecting that figure to rise to $70 billion by year-end, according to one of the people.

OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the person added.   Anthropic's annualized revenue reached roughly $65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to $16.8 billion in the third quarter from $11.6 billion in the second quarter this year, it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth has raised concerns among investors about its valuation.   OpenAI is seeking to complete the fundraising before Anthropic's financial disclosures give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said.

The disclosures could prompt investors to press OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company's revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier that it follows established accounting practices.   "OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison)," said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. "It's really a two-horse race in terms of being public."

OpenAI was last valued at $852 billion in March this year, after a record-breaking $122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to $50 billion in the lab.   The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI's potential fundraising.  IPO PLANS HIT BY MARKET JITTERS   A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic's planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks, bankers and investors said. Some late-stage companies are also timing private fundraising rounds to avoid coinciding with Anthropic's expected debut, the bankers and investors said.

Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued for a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion for its market debut - instead of the desired $2 trillion - after the AI startup's third-quarter results fell short of expectations, Reuters reported last week.   The reassessment comes amid a choppy market since September, with volatility in oil prices, rising bond yields and growing concerns about AI safety weighing on investor appetite for technology stocks. Investors are also scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure, including the debt needed to finance the data centers powering the boom.   At the center of the latest concerns is cloud provider CoreWeave, whose shares and debt tumbled last week as investors scrutinized the nearly $50 billion in borrowings used to fund its rapid expansion.

The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans amid market volatility and concerns about valuations. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia -backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings.   Nuclear services company Holtec cited a "perfect storm," driven mainly by uncertainty around data-center demand, when it pulled its US listing last month.   Companies in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, widely viewed as a proxy for AI-related semiconductor demand, have shed $1.6 trillion in less than two weeks, while AI infrastructure companies have come under particular pressure.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: India flags high unpaid UN dues, raises concern over 2026 liquidity crunch
item.description: India has voiced concern over the "challenging" liquidity situation of the United Nations this year, as it called out the "unacceptably high levels" of unpaid assessments owed by just one member state ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / India flags high unpaid UN dues, raises concern over 2026 liquidity crunch

India flags high unpaid UN dues, raises concern over 2026 liquidity crunch India has raised concern over the UN's liquidity pressures, noting that unpaid regular budget assessments stood at $1.46 billion in 2026, with more than 90% owed by a single member state

Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India United Nations 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:23 AM IST

Listen to This Article

India has voiced concern over the "challenging" liquidity situation of the United Nations this year, as it called out the "unacceptably high levels" of unpaid assessments owed by just one member state. "We consider that full, timely and unconditional payment of assessed contribution is the Charter obligation of every Member State," Counsellor in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Surendra Adhana said here Monday. Adhana delivered India's national statement at the 81st Main Session of the Fifth Committee of the UN General Assembly on 'Improving the financial situation of the United Nations'. "We note with concern that the liquidity situation in 2026 remained challenging due to the collection uncertainties and low cash balance," he said.

"While we have noted the marginal drop in the regular budget unpaid assessment to $1.46 billion from the $1.87 billion a year ago, the reality is that the unpaid assessment continued to remain at unacceptably high levels, and over 90 per cent of the regular budget arrears are owed by one member state," he said. Also Read

India urges vigilance on weapons tech transfers to terror-linked actors

Banks tap RBI's first cash auction in 3 months as market rates spike

India rejects UN expert's report on youth freedom, asks to verify claims

The US is the single largest financial contributor to the UN, paying 22 per cent of the regular budget and 27per cent of the peacekeeping budget. In September, Washington paid $725 million to the UN regular budget and an additional $102 million for peacekeeping. But the US still owes the UN over $4 billion for its regular budget and peacekeeping arrears.

Adhana noted that the respite resulting from a strong collection in the third quarter needs to be sustained. India welcomed that 141 member states had paid in full their assessment by September 30 this year compared to 136 member states last year. India also voiced concern over the financial situation in UN peacekeeping, describing it as "more worrisome". Adhana noted that unpaid assessments for UN peacekeeping reached $4.1 billion, up from $3.7 billion last year, while collection stagnated at around 1.4 billion. "Two member states alone account for roughly 88 per cent of this amount," he said. US and China are the top two contributors to UN peacekeeping. China paid $641.4 million in September for its regular UN budget contributions.

"We urge all Member States, especially those with requisite means, to take expeditious action to fulfill their financial obligations. This is critical to ensuring a financially healthy and sound United Nations with zero indebtedness. It is an integral part of our common quest for prudent budgetary and financial management of the organisation," he said. India has consistently paid its assessment in full, on time, and often in advance. This year, India was among the 55 Member States that paid their regular budget assessments in full within the 30 day due period. India made a payment of $35.18 million in February this year.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
